*"Don't you miss having a strong man's shoulder to lean on?"* asked Rebecca223, for a hundred dollars. *"Would you give up your business if you met the love of your life?"*

Freya decided to answer.

"A business can't replace a man, and a man can't replace your life's work. Though a business doesn't need pleasing the way a lover does. And the right business will *always* stand up for you." Here Freya smiled. "Which, you have to admit, gives it a clear edge over a man."

The chats exploded. The Twitter and Instagram feeds on the side monitors raced like mad. The feminist community kicked into full gear, and the feed suddenly bloomed with avatars sporting rainbow-colored hair, like an exotic greenhouse. Now it wasn't her assistants but Freya's fans themselves who were filing reports and slinging mud at the right-wingers who had swarmed to the light of her stream from their anonymous loser forums. The right-wingers were always a lot of trouble.

Still, three hundred eighty... no, three hundred ninety thousand live viewers were three hundred ninety thousand live viewers. No matter what they smelled like.

The trolls tried to flood the stream with questions like *"Do you swallow?"* and *"Try shaving your legs"*: zero imagination, but plenty of volume. Dumb green sad frogs started popping up in the chat. Freya kept smiling and answering questions selectively, glancing at her assistants' chat. Whichever way you sliced it, the comments set the tone. As it turned out, though, the moderators weren't needed.

The trolls' moms never gave them more than five dollars for school lunch. So they were crushed by a counterattack from the very core of Freya's audience, rallied by the call of her fan groups on Twitter, TikTok, and Instagram. Stay-at-home moms, manicurists, and girls from provincial colleges rushed to their idol's rescue. Housewives who, at the loud summons of the modern economy, had traded their ladles for enormous smartphones. And men who craved the attention of all the aforementioned women, and so had started passing themselves off as "one of them," without even noticing they were blowing twenty bucks a month on Freya, sometimes more.

Not the best audience if you're a serious woman sharing the secrets of *real* success, but a loyal one. And in real business, loyalty counts for a lot.

Right before Freya's eyes, the haters' comments were washed away by twenty- and fifty-dollar messages: *"Go, Freya!", "Freya, we love you!", "#Axelsensexuals!"* The stakes climbed fast, and soon donations under ten dollars weren't even showing up on screen. At last, the girl smiled for real.
